subjects.introduction: How does a human soul become something other than it was, and what do the Writings say makes that change possible? These 300 chosen quotations include every verified authorized selection in the compilation. They begin with the Divine Springtime of the Manifestation and the Elixir that transmutes base metal into gold, then follow the awakening of sleepers and the quickening of the dead, the second birth and the iron that takes on the qualities of fire. Later readings consider the capacity a heart must acquire, growth through stages, tests as a refining fire, and the evidence of a changed character, before turning to education, to the transformation of others and the world, and closing with prayers. Passages come from Bahá’u’lláh, the Báb and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, with reported talks and secondary accounts among them; supplied wording follows at the end with its catalogue status.
subjects.arc: The Divine Springtime → The Divine Elixir → Sleepers awakened → The second birth → Iron in the fire → The receptive heart → Stages of growth → The refining fire → A changed character → Nurture and education → Light for the world → Prayers for transformation

order.why: These readings begin with the source of transformation. In the Kitáb-i-Íqán Bahá’u’lláh asks whether the object of every Revelation is not to effect a transformation in the whole character of mankind, both outwardly and inwardly. He announces that the Divine Springtime is come, and observes how many trees of human souls have become fresh and verdant in this springtide while others in the same season have withered. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that Bahá’u’lláh has renewed that springtime, with the same fragrances, the same heat of the Sun and the same cloud, and that when the Manifestation casts His splendour on hearts a spiritual springtime is ushered in. Reported talks call the Teachings the breaths of the Holy Spirit that create men anew. Why do the Writings place the beginning of transformation in the coming of a Manifestation rather than in individual effort? What does the image of spring suggest about how such change happens?

He announces that the Divine Springtime is come, and observes how many trees of human souls have become fresh and verdant in this springtide while others in the same season have withered. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that Bahá’u’lláh has renewed that springtime, with the same fragrances, the same heat of the Sun and the same cloud, and that when the Manifestation casts His splendour on hearts a spiritual springtime is ushered in. Reported talks call the Teachings the breaths of the Holy Spirit that create men anew. Why do the Writings place the beginning of transformation in the coming of a Manifestation rather than in individual effort? What does the image of spring suggest about how such change happens?

These readings take up the Divine Elixir. Bahá’u’lláh speaks of His most exalted Word, ordained as the Divine Elixir through whose potency the crude metal of human life has been transmuted into purest gold, and of a few who have been endued with that Elixir and with the infallible remedy for the ills of men. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá asks the friends to find the Alchemy of Truth and cast it upon the copper and iron of men’s souls, and says the Prophets appear so that the lump of coal may become a diamond. Through divine power the mosquito becomes an eagle, the shell a pearl and dust the philosopher’s stone. Beside the elixir stands the remedy: no disease is greater than heedlessness and hate, and no remedy more potent than the Word of God. What does the language of alchemy say that the language of improvement cannot? Why must patients first be made aware of their illness?

These readings describe awakening and the quickening of the dead. Bahá’u’lláh prays, I lay asleep on the bed of self when lo, Thou didst waken me with the divine accents of Thy voice, and says that He found man asleep and awakened him, distant and drew him near, mute and caused him to speak. By graves, He explains, is meant heedlessness of self and passion, a death more severe than physical death; and he who walks and speaks may be counted among the dead. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá recalls Christ’s words, Let the dead bury the dead, describes souls dead in the graves of desire raised by the trumpet blast of the Abhá Kingdom, and a reported talk notes that some wake at a touch while others need the noise of a cannon. Prayers ask, I am earthly; make me heavenly. What distinguishes outward life from the life these passages mean? What might it take to wake a heavy sleeper?

These readings turn to the second birth. Reported talks recall Christ’s saying, Ye must be born again, and explain that as a child is born from the womb of its mother into this world, so a soul is born out of the world of nature into the world of the spirit through divine education. The embryo is alive but counted as dead until it is born, and the pain of birth is a gift. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of baptism with the water of life, the fire of the love of God and the Holy Spirit, and defines eternal life as receiving the grace of the Holy Spirit, as a flower receives the breezes of spring. Bahá’u’lláh writes that the life mentioned in the Books of the Prophets is the life of knowledge. You must be newly created, one talk says; your very being must be transformed. What does the analogy of birth teach about the powers a soul receives before it can use them? Can a second birth happen gradually?

These readings consider capacity and the purified heart. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that however mighty the outpouring of grace, souls must become receptive and worthy; a reported talk adds that the mirror must be cleared of rust before the sun is reflected, as one prepares the apartment before inviting the guest. Stone and clay may lie in fire a thousand years without effect while the wick of a lamp blazes at a touch, and a black stone cannot become a ruby. Reported talks ask that the soil of hearts be freed of weeds and thorns, and say that capacity grows through detachment from the world and attraction to God. Bahá’u’lláh writes that all He has endured has one purpose, that hearts may be sanctified from selfish inclinations, and that the fast decreases the carnal and increases the spiritual; the Báb asks that the earth of souls be purified. Is capacity given or acquired? What in these passages prepares a heart to receive?

These readings describe transformation as growth through stages. Bahá’u’lláh counsels, In every breath be other than thy former self, and with every step advance beyond thy previous step, and describes seas of search, love and detachment. The Báb calls the whole Law a path for the servant to journey toward his Lord and traces how knowledge leads to fear, fear to flight and flight to salvation. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes progress in station from progress in perfections and hopes that a drop may expand day by day into a boundless ocean. Reported talks say that the soul evolves only nearer to God, liken the spirit to a muscle strengthened by exercise, advise comparing today with yesterday each morning, and warn that stagnation is the beginning of retrogression. At the gate of the garden some look in and only a few penetrate. What makes spiritual progress measurable, if anything? Why is standing still described as falling back?

Bahá’u’lláh testifies that His countenance has been irradiated by adversity and that the friends of God win under all conditions. How can the same hardship refine one soul and break another? What do these readings ask of a person in the middle of a test?

These readings look for transformation in character and conduct. Bahá’u’lláh hopes that each may adorn himself with pure and holy deeds, calls striving with one’s own self the greater striving, and asks that once the heart is purified the believer act on the Tablets so that the outward temple too becomes pure. Reported talks describe a person who remains the same in form but in character has become another, observe that a moral teacher may labour to remove one fault while the dawning of faith changes a person wholly, ask that quick temper be changed into calmness and pride into humility, insist on complete regeneration rather than a change of name, and say of one transformed believer that she is the proof of Bahá’u’lláh. Narratives tell of Gregory, of Mírzá ‘Alí-Akbar re-created within minutes, and of Abu Dharr and Bilal. How can others recognize a changed life? Which qualities in these accounts change first?

Reported talks describe a person who remains the same in form but in character has become another, observe that a moral teacher may labour to remove one fault while the dawning of faith changes a person wholly, ask that quick temper be changed into calmness and pride into humility, insist on complete regeneration rather than a change of name, and say of one transformed believer that she is the proof of Bahá’u’lláh. Narratives tell of Gregory, of Mírzá ‘Alí-Akbar re-created within minutes, and of Abu Dharr and Bilal. How can others recognize a changed life? Which qualities in these accounts change first?

These readings treat transformation as nurture and education. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá writes to children as saplings grown in the garden of the love of God and prays that tender plants become verdant through the clouds of mercy. He hopes that education will transform earthly children into heavenly youths, and that children fostered in the shell of education will grow like pearls of divine bounty. He asks the friends to train the souls of men until frenzied beasts change to gazelles and wolves to lambs. Why do these passages give the educator so large a part? What is the difference between training and transformation?

These readings carry transformation from the soul to others and to the world. Reported talks say that wherever purified, severed and illumined souls are found, there is the paradise of Bahá, and that a new era of divine consciousness has come in which the world of humanity is passing through a process of transformation. They describe the centres around which most human thought revolves, egoism, selfishness and cupidity, and ask that the divine forces be let loose to change them. One who has been educated by the Divine Spirit can lead others to receive the same Spirit, and in giving the Message we develop ourselves: the more we give, the more we receive. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá assures one who arises with all his power that he will guide souls unto the wellspring of life and quicken them with the breaths of the All-Merciful. How is the transformation of one person connected with the transformation of society? What do these passages say a changed soul owes to others?

The supplied quotation stops before the clause on the world becoming the Kingdom of God; the approximate status is preserved. Compare it with the readings on awakening and on transforming others. What birthright is meant here?

This supplied provisional rendering of a Tablet of ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that God rejects distinctions of race and border, that all the divine teachings aim at improving human character, and that only the power of the Holy Spirit can transform man, bestowing the second birth and baptizing him with the fire of the love of God, which is love for all created things. The catalogue renders the same paragraphs differently, and neither rendering is authorized; the approximate status is preserved. Why does this passage tie the second birth to love for all creation?

questions: The readings describe transformation through many images: spring, alchemy, birth, waking, iron in the fire. Choose two of these images and compare them. What does each reveal about the change that the other does not?

Some passages say the change can happen in an instant, more swiftly than the twinkling of an eye; others describe slow growth through stages, day by day. How can both be true, and what do the narratives in the section on character suggest?

Many readings insist that grace is mighty but souls must become receptive and worthy. What part do the readings give to divine power and what part to human effort? Look at the wick and the stone, the polished mirror, and the counsel to compare today with yesterday.

Why do so many passages connect transformation with tests and suffering? Consider the soil that is ploughed, gold in the fire and winter before spring, and ask what the readings say a person should do during a test.

The Kitáb-i-Íqán says that a Revelation should transform the character of mankind both outwardly and inwardly. What signs of inward change do the readings describe, and how do they say it should appear in conduct, in families and in society?
Several prayers ask God to make the one who prays heavenly, pure or detached. How might praying in this way take part in the process the other readings describe?
